description: We're building a public-facing web tool that lets anyone explore NASA's SPHEREx all-sky data, spotting comets, asteroids, stars, and hidden planets as they shift across billions of infrared images over time.
summary:
AURAx is a public-facing web application that helps people explore how the infrared sky changes over time using real NASA SPHEREx observations. Users enter sky coordinates or search for a named object, retrieve target-centred images, and compare two to four observations through aligned views and animated playback.

To support responsible exploration, AURAx displays observation dates, wavelength information, data-quality flags, and coverage warnings. Its checked blink mode applies stricter comparison requirements, helping users distinguish possible astronomical changes from wavelength differences or unusable pixels. Small cutouts and controlled loading reduce unnecessary downloads.

We tested image retrieval and registration around all five challenge targets and developed a checked Epsilon Indi B time-comparison example. AURAx makes archive data more approachable for students, educators, and citizen scientists while preserving the evidence and limitations needed to investigate possible changes.
details:
AURAx — Explore the Changing Infrared Sky

AURAx is a public-facing web application for exploring real NASA SPHEREx observations and comparing how a patch of sky appears at different times. It brings coordinate search, image inspection, animated comparison, and scientific context into one accessible workspace.

EXPLORE THE PROJECT

Live application:
https://aurax.thawshi.com

Interactive user guide:
https://aurax.thawshi.com/docs

Source code and project README:

Supporting materials:
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/16kaDiCB-tFyycD5B6L1ZEZ3-a3SuzLoH?usp=drive_link


1. Demonstration video:

2. Full walkthrough

WHAT USERS CAN DO

Users enter right ascension and declination or search for an object by name. AURAx resolves named objects through SIMBAD, searches NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx observations covering the selected position, and retrieves calibrated FITS cutouts.

The Images workspace lets users inspect individual observations, adjust the display, examine metadata and quality flags, and investigate selected image regions. Saved targets let users return to their selections and retrieve available nearest-pixel spectral samples with uncertainties. These samples include background light and are not complete source spectra.

The comparison workspace supports two to four observations in aligned views and animated playback. Users can filter and select observations, control playback speed, and inspect each frame’s date, detector, wavelength information, and usable coverage.

General comparisons allow exploration across wavelengths, with warnings explaining their interpretation. A separate checked blink workflow applies stricter wavelength, registration, and quality requirements for comparisons over time.

HOW TO TRY IT

  1. Open the live application.
  2. Choose a challenge target or enter sky coordinates.
  3. Browse available observations and inspect a small cutout.
  4. Select observations for comparison and choose Analyse.
  5. Play or step through the prepared frames, checking their dates, wavelengths, and quality information.
  6. For a documented time-comparison example, open the checked Epsilon Indi B example from Home.

REAL OBSERVATIONS AND VISUAL EVIDENCE

We tested retrieval and registration of four real SPHEREx observations around each required challenge target: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Our checked Epsilon Indi B example uses two observations separated by approximately 509 days, with closely matched target wavelengths. An exploratory displacement check is consistent with the source’s catalog motion.

Two-frame animation:

Animation caption: Two real, registered SPHEREx observations of the Epsilon Indi B field, displayed with identical scaling. The cyan marker indicates a fixed sky coordinate; blue pixels are excluded. No intermediate observations are synthesized.

Reference-check figure:

Figure caption: The wider field and target-region crops used for an exploratory displacement check. Orange circles mark approximate catalog expectations; cyan crosses mark exploratory centroids. This is a known-motion illustration, not precision astrometry or a new discovery.

Reproducible example and limitations:


https://github.com/Thawshi-Srikanth/01-AuraX-2026/blob/main/docs/epsilon-indi-example-validation-2026-11-15.md

DESIGNED FOR RESPONSIBLE EXPLORATION

AURAx defaults to small, target-centred cutouts of approximately 50 pixels per side, with larger options available. Selected observations load sequentially, and caching reduces repeated downloads.

If an IRSA TAP metadata request fails, AURAx can attempt the official IRSA SIA service. Both routes depend on archive availability. Persistent failures are reported rather than replaced with invented observations.

The application preserves timestamps, data references, wavelength information, quality flags, and masks. It distinguishes missing or unusable pixels from valid measurements.

Retrieving an image does not prove that a target is detected or measurable. Some selected stellar cores are masked, and wavelength differences, background emission, and instrument effects can change an image’s appearance. AURAx makes these limitations visible so users can investigate possible changes carefully.

DOCUMENTATION

The in-app guide covers:

  • Your first observation.
  • How light becomes an image.
  • Right ascension, declination, and coordinate epochs.
  • Brightness and flux.
  • Wavelengths and detector position.
  • Image registration and careful time comparison.
  • Archive access and caching.

User guide:
https://aurax.thawshi.com/docs

Challenge objective audit and five-target validation:
https://github.com/Thawshi-Srikanth/01-AuraX-2026/blob/main/docs/challenge-audit-2026-11-15.md

https://github.com/Thawshi-Srikanth/01-AuraX-2026/blob/main/docs/deployment.md

NASA image sources and credits:
https://github.com/Thawshi-Srikanth/01-AuraX-2026/blob/main/frontend/public/assets/home/CREDITS.md

TECHNOLOGY

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and browser canvas rendering.

The Python backend uses FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, PyVO, Reproject, and Photutils. SQLite and local FITS storage support caching.

Docker Compose, Nginx, and GitHub Actions support deployment and automated verification.

OpenAI ChatGPT & Gemini assisted with implementation, debugging, testing, interface refinement, and documentation. Scientific observations come from archive products; AI-generated observations are not substituted for unavailable data.

CREATIVITY AND INTENDED IMPACT

AURAx combines a beginner-friendly exploration workflow with the information needed to question an apparent change. Users can move from a sky coordinate to real observations, inspect a sequence, and understand why a comparison may or may not support a scientific interpretation.

The Sky View

The intended audience includes students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists. Our goal is to make SPHEREx observations easier to explore while preserving their provenance and scientific limitations.
